results.title: Palaeoclimate, environmental factors, and bird body size: A multivariable analysis of avian fossil preservation - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Invited review Palaeoclimate, environmental factors, and bird body size: A multivariable analysis of avian fossil preservation. For this study, we abstracted data on 693 avian fossil specimens from 398 publications to determine preservation biases in the avian fossil record. Our results show that dissociated wing and leg bones are the most commonly preserved avian skeletal elements and they are preferentially preserved in environments of high erosion and reworking potential—notably continental shelf marine environments. Using bivariate descriptive displays and multivariable regression analyses, we investigated the trends and associations between well-preserved avian specimens (i.e., fully- or partially-articulated) and a variety of taphonomic factors, including depositional environment, body size, and palaeoclimate. Warm climates, the strongest predictor of better skeletal preservation, may be underestimated as a source of taphonomic bias in the avian fossil record, possibly because of the indirect nature of climate effects. Our analyses indicate that geologic processes leading to high quality preservation of avian fossils are closely associated with climate. In the past twenty years, there has been a surge of publications reporting new or better preserved avian fossils, yet the taphonomic factors that affect avian preservation in the fossil record remain little studied. The Amboseli results suggest that robust skeletal elements may be over-represented in the fossil record as compared to smaller bird bones. Overall, modern studies have reported differing rates of avian decay, skeletal disarticulation, and bone loss in disparate environments, but they have not clearly compared their experimental results with the avian fossil record for either climate or body size factors. Microstructural characteristics of bird bones may also be an important factor in their decay and weathering: avian bones vary in structure by the age and sex of the bird, as well as by individual skeletal elements (Schufeldt, 1902). The influences of climate and bird body size on preservation potential are much less well-studied in the avian fossil record than aspects of the depositional environment, such as sediment type and sediment transport energy. The Las Hoyas limestones of Cuenca, Spain, also have excellently preserved avian fossils resulting from the accumulation of fine-grained carbonate sediments in anoxic bottom waters, which precluded disarticulation and bacterial decay (Sanz et al., 1988).

results.title: Decomposition in Aquatic Environments: Forensic Analysis of the Dead and the Depositional Environment
results.content: In this review, previous research surrounding human remains in the marine environment is reviewed with a focus on the factors that will influence decomposition of the human body from initial submergence to skeletonization. Outdoor human decomposition in Sweden: A retrospective quantitative study of forensic-taphonomic changes and postmortem interval in terrestrial and aquatic settings. Wet depositional conditions can affect and obscure the timing of breakage through changed decomposition rates (Haglund and Sorg, 2002;Augias et al., 2017;Stuart and Ueland, 2017), alterations in the breakage behavior of dry bone after rehydration (Broz et al., 1993;Moraitis and Spiliopoulou, 2006;Augias et al., 2017;King, 2017), and the increased abrasion of character-istic breakage edges in water environments (Haglund and Sorg, 2002;Moraitis and Spiliopoulou, 2006). In addition, this chapter presents methods of estimating the postmortem submergence interval (PMSI) in these environments, including degree of decomposition and the stage of marine abrasion and other accrued taphonomic effects on exposed bones. Bodies in sequestered and non-sequestered aquatic environments: A comparative taphonomic study using decompositional scoring system. In order to verify how useful can the total aquatic decomposition score (TADS) for ADD prediction be, a comparative taphonomic study has been performed between two series of bodies: 16 corpses found floating in shallower waters with a presumptive PMSI from 3 to 118 days and exposed to water temperatures (Tw) between 10.5 and 20.3 °C approximately equating from a minimum of 46 to 1.392 ADD; 52 bodies, all victims of a single shipwreck, found in sequestered environments and subjected to constant Tw of 4 °C for 210 days approximately equating to 840 ADD. Empirical data on postmortem aquatic changes may be extremely useful in forensic contexts for both improving time since death estimates and also for providing better information to underwater recovery experts thereby potentially increasing the quantity and quality of remains recovery. This study aimed to investigate the microbes involved in decomposition in the sea and to evaluate the potential use of marine bacterial succession for postmortem submersion interval (PMSI) estimation, for which there is currently no reliable method. results.title: Syn-depositional alteration of coral reef framework through bioerosion, encrustation and cementation: Taphonomic signatures of reef accretion and reef depositional events - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Syn-depositional alteration of coral reef framework through bioerosion, encrustation and cementation: Taphonomic signatures of reef accretion and reef depositional events. The development of coral reef framework and the preservational character of both in-situ and rubble coral is strongly influenced by a range of physical, chemical and biologically-mediated taphonomic processes. These processes, taken in the broadest sense of the term ‘reef taphonomy’, encompass not only coral growth and deposition, but also near surface alteration of the primary framework constituents, and the effects of post-burial diagenesis. In terms of the development of a coral reef these varied taphonomic processes, most of which operate at, or just below, the reef framework: water interface, are important because they exert a strong influence on the composition of coral material entering the fossil record (Pandolfi and Greenstein, 1997, Greenstein and Pandolfi, 2003) and because they influence the nature of reef framework development. Within coral reef environments a number of important groups/processes that exert a taphonomic influence on the primary reef fabric fulfil, to varying degrees, these criteria. Given this, the primary objectives of this paper are to: (1) review our current understanding of the distribution of key species/groups/processes that operate in the reef environment and which exert a taphonomic influence upon primary reef framework components within Holocene coral reef environments; (2) to identify the suites of taphonomic signatures that can be regarded as indicative of different reef sub-environments; and (3) to identify the taphonomic signatures that are indicative of reef depositional styles and events over a range of temporal scales. ## Distribution of taphonomic groups/processes within Holocene coral reef environments. The discussion in Section 2 provides a strong case to support the view that different reef sub-environments can be broadly characterised by various suites of taphonomic signatures and by environmentally-controlled shifts in the types and relative abundance of key species that play a role in the taphonomic modification of coral framework constituents. Carbonate reef substrates are typically subject to a high degree of taphonomic alteration, the majority of which is associated with the effects of four main groups of organisms and/or reef-related processes; calcareous encrustation, micro- and macroendolithic boring, and marine cementation.
